catalog_quote: Before turning to the main topic of the paper, adjectives, I briefly lay out the morphophonological structure of the language. Seenku has undergone extensive reduction, leaving the vocabulary largely mono- and sesquisyllabic, a term generally reserved for Southeast Asian languages (Matisoff 1990, Brunelle and Pittayaporn 2012, Butler 2014). In other words, where many other Mande languages see reduction or deletion of certain vowels in certain stress positions (e.g. initial unstressed high vowels in an iambic foot, Bambara, Green 2010), these reduction patterns in Seenku have resulted in restructuring and concurrent loss of the stress system, with the original full vowels ostensibly no longer part of the underlying representation. As seen in (1a), monosyllabic words can have either a short or long vowel, with or without a coda nasal.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Seenku is a four-level tone language (X, L, H, S plus contours); the author states that the historical vowel reductions that produced its mono- and sesquisyllabic vocabulary came with the loss of the (Mande iambic-foot) stress system, so no synchronic word-stress rule is posited — word prosody is tonal only.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the remark is a passing statement in a morphosyntax paper, and the dedicated phonetic description (JIPA 2020 Illustration) does not discuss stress at all.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (lexical vocabulary); the sesquisyllabic half-syllable is not a tone-bearing unit. Data are from the Southern dialect (Bouendé/Gbeneku), author's fieldwork 2012-2016.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data (McPherson 2017, 2019, 2020 JIPA, 2021) describe the Southern dialect (Gbeneku, village of Bouendé/Gbene, ~11-12k speakers); Prost 1971 describes the Northern dialect (Timiku, Karangasso, ~5k). Glottolog 5.1 seek1238 is the language-level node and lists no dialect glottocodes (its reference records label the varieties 'Sembla of Bouendé / Southern Seeku' and 'Sembla of Karangasso / Northern Seeku').

tone_statements.quote: This morphosyntactic simplicity is counterbalanced by a highly complex tone system. Seenku displays four contrastive levels of tone, as evidenced by the near- minimal set in Table 1. … Tone Example Gloss Super-high (S) sı ̋ ‘tree sp.’ High (H) (í) sí reciprocal Low (L) sì ‘first son’ (proper name) Extra-low (X) sȉ ‘water jar’ These four tones can combine to create a wide array of two- and three-tone contours, including HX (e.g., bî ‘goat’) … there is clear evidence that these contour tones are composed of combinations of level tones

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2021. Categoricity, Variation, and Gradience in Sambla Balafon Segmental Encoding. Frontiers in Communication 6: 652635. doi:10.3389/fcomm.2021.652635 (CC BY 4.0).
tone_statements.quote: Seenku has four contrastive tone levels, which I call Superhigh (S), High (H), Low (L), and Extralow (X), marked with double acute (a̋), acute (á), grave (à) and double grave (ȁ) diacritics, respectively. The four tone levels are distinguished solely by f0, with no significant role played by vowel length or phonation. A minimal set for level tones is shown in (1) … These four level tones can combine to create a vast array of two- and three-tone contours. The most common lexical contours are HX (â), LS (ǎ), and HS (áa)̋ …
tone_statements.locator: p. 3, section 'Background on Sambla Music and the Seenku Language' > 'Seenku Phonology' > 'Tonal Inventory', example (1) and the contour paragraph following Table 2
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive level tones (superhigh, high, low, extralow) distinguished by f0 alone; contours such as HX, LS, HS are combinations of the levels; lexical and grammatical tone; tone sandhi noted.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2018 [publ. 2019]. The Talking Balafon of the Sambla: Grammatical Principles and Documentary Implications. Anthropological Linguistics 60(3): 255-294. doi:10.1353/anl.2019.0006.
tone_statements.quote: While word structure will play a role in the surrogate language, by far the most important phonological aspect is tone. Seenku’s tone system is one of the most complex in the region. Unlike its immediate neighbors and the other Samogo languages (to the best of our knowledge), there are four contrasting levels of tone, which I call extra-low X (ȁ), low L (à), high H (á), and super-high S (a̋ ). … These four levels can combine to create almost every possible two-tone contour tone, though only a small number of these are underlying … Lexically, HX, HS, and LS are the most common contour tones
tone_statements.locator: MS pp. 15-16 (page numbers), sec. 3.3 'The Sambla language: Seenku', exx. (3)-(4)
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive level tones (extra-low, low, high, super-high) on the syllable; contours (HX, HS, LS, XHX) are combinations of levels, few underlying; downstepped S; heavy grammatical tone.

tone_statements.quote: The tone system of the language is very complex, with 4 contrastive levels and 12 simple and complex contour tones (of which 4 are lexical and the other grammatical). The 4 level tones are illustrated in (1): (1) a. Extra-low (X) sȁn ‘river’ b. Low (L) sà ‘second-born son’ c. High (H) sá ‘cry’ d. Super-high (S) sa̋ n ‘God’ The contour tones HX and LS are the most common two-tone lexical contours, followed by HS: … The tri-tone contour XHX is also attested lexically … The half syllable of sesquisyllabic words is not tonally contrastive …
tone_statements.locator: p. 63, §3.1.1 'Seenku phonology', exx. (1)-(2); f0 statement p. 64 §5.1 'Four contrastive levels'
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive level tones (extra-low, low, high, super-high) plus 12 lexical/grammatical contours built from them (HX, LS, HS, XHX); half syllables not tonally contrastive; southern dialect.

tone_statements.citation: McPherson, Laura. 2017. Multiple feature affixation in Seenku plural formation. Morphology 27.
tone_statements.quote: Seenku is a four-tone language, contrasting the levels X (extra low), L (low), H (high), and S (super high). However, as we will see, L is largely confined to derived forms, such as the plural. These tones can also combine into numerous contour tones, including H-X, S-X, L-S, X-H-X, L-S-X, and H-S. The Tone Bearing Unit (TBU) is the syllable, and each syllable can host up to three tones, though I have only seen this latter situation on long vowels. If a rising tone or tritone sequence is applied grammatically on a light syllable, the vowel typically lengthens to accommodate it.

sources.quote: The tone system of the language is very complex, with 4 contrastive levels and 12 simple and complex contour tones (of which 4 are lexical and the other grammatical). The 4 level tones are illustrated in (1): (1) a. Extra-low (X) sȁn ‘river’ b. Low (L) sà ‘second-born son’ c. High (H) sá ‘cry’ d. Super-high (S) sa̋ n ‘God’ The contour tones HX and LS are the most common two-tone lexical contours, followed by HS: … The tri-tone contour XHX is also attested lexically … The half syllable of sesquisyllabic words is not tonally contrastive …

sources.quote: Seenku is a four-tone language, contrasting the levels X (extra low), L (low), H (high), and S (super high). However, as we will see, L is largely confined to derived forms, such as the plural. These tones can also combine into numerous contour tones, including H-X, S-X, L-S, X-H-X, L-S-X, and H-S. The Tone Bearing Unit (TBU) is the syllable, and each syllable can host up to three tones, though I have only seen this latter situation on long vowels. If a rising tone or tritone sequence is applied grammatically on a light syllable, the vowel typically lengthens to accommodate it.
